title: The questions left
tomorrow: Eli whispers he's not sure God exists. can he still read Torah?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rashi's note on the first verse: interpret me. Your own margin. Today, what to do when your note is a question nobody can answer.
screen: `YOUR OWN MARGIN.` → `A QUESTION NOBODY CAN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: A kid asks the question you can't answer, and your face does the thing. Good question, you say, and change the subject. Not knowing can feel like failing the job. But the Talmud sometimes fails the job on purpose. The rabbis argue a case back and forth, and the passage ends with one word: teiku. It stands. Unresolved. Left on the page, and the discussion moves on. So does a teacher have to answer? Two great voices in the tradition lean different ways.
screen: `GOOD QUESTION. NEXT.` → `TEIKU: IT STANDS.` → `TWO VOICES, TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: The first voice is the Talmud's own way, and the Mishnah says why. In the tractate Eduyot, it asks: why record the opinion that lost? And it answers: so that a later court can find it and rely on it someday. The minority view is kept. The open question is kept. Its best case: the conversation is bigger than any one generation, and the next learner may see what you can't. The second voice is Maimonides. In the introduction to his great code, the Mishneh Torah, he says he gathered the law clearly, so that a person could read the Torah, then his book, and know what to do, without needing another book in between. His best case: people have to live today. A family deciding how to keep Shabbat needs an answer, not a shelf of debates. Here's what the tradition did with both. It kept the Talmud with its teiku. It kept Maimonides' code. And later scholars printed their objections in the margins of his code, right next to his rulings. Answers and questions on the same page. So the honest teacher's move might be: here's what we do, and here's what we still don't know. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Mishnah keeps the losing argument on purpose, in case it's needed later.
screen: `WHY RECORD THE OPINION THAT LOST?` · `MAIMONIDES: KNOW WHAT TO DO.` · `BOTH KEPT, ON ONE PAGE.` · `WHAT WE DO, WHAT WE DON'T KNOW.` · then, large: `QUESTIONS LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: Write a short list of three questions you still carry about this path: one about a text, one about a practice, and one about meaning, or God, if that's yours. Don't answer them. Beside each one, write the word: stands.
The questions left: what every learner keeps after the lesson ends. The Talmud has a word for them, teiku, and it leaves them standing.
Keep this one: questions left open; in the Talmud, teiku is a real ending too. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish learners study the Talmud with its open questions and minority views, and also turn to codes of law, such as Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, for what to do in practice.

chat.says: eli asked why God would need to rest. i said "great question" and panicked. am i a fraud?
options: Not a fraud. Say you don't know yet; the Talmud leaves questions standing too.
A little. A teacher should always have the answer ready, or he'll stop trusting you.
Look it up fast and hand him the one official answer. There's always one.
chat.meaning: The Talmud sometimes ends a debate with teiku: it stands. An honest teacher can say what we do and what we still don't know.

teiku.meaning: Aramaic: it stands; a question the Talmud leaves unresolved

Maimonides.meaning: a medieval Jewish scholar, physician and author of a law code

Mishnah.meaning: an early written collection of the rabbis' teachings

notes: Teiku glossed as 'it stands'; the popular acronym reading (Elijah will resolve questions) is deliberately left out under the claims rule. Confirm the example reference (Bava Metzia 8b) or substitute a better one.
Mishnah Eduyot 1:5 paraphrased: the minority view is recorded so a later court may rely on it. Confirm.
Maimonides' introduction to the Mishneh Torah paraphrased: read the Written Torah, then this book, and know the whole Oral Torah without needing another book between them. Confirm.
'Later scholars printed their objections in the margins of his code' refers to the hasagot of the Raavad and others printed beside the Mishneh Torah. Confirm phrasing.
Debate day: the two views (keep the open question; give a clear ruling) are let to speak, ranking neither.
